53:2.text: And it came to pass, when he had made an end of speaking unto Saul, that the soul of Jonathan was knit with the soul of David, and Jonathan loved him as his own soul.

provenance.other: “knit with the soul” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, 1 Samuel 18:1, and “loved him as his own soul” in exactly two, 1 Samuel 18:1 and 18:3 — the same episode. Alma 53:2 reproduces none of this; its words are 'they rejoiced in each other's safety; yea, they were beloved by each other'. The row is filed on the situation and on the company it keeps in this chapter, not on a string.
provenance.alternative: Two commanders fond of one another is not a scene that needs a source, and the Book of Mormon's language for it is its own.
provenance.significance: The KJV has one friendship between fighting men that it troubles to describe as love, and it describes it in the chapter immediately after the giant is killed — Jonathan's soul knit to David's, a covenant made, and the elder man handing over his own equipment. Alma 53:2 gives Lehi the same standing beside Moroni: 'he was a man like unto Moroni', with him in the more part of his battles, and the transfer that occasions the sentence is Moroni taking the city and giving it to Lehi. Read with the rest of the chapter the reading firms up considerably: 53:20 gives the young men Saul's charge to David ('be thou valiant for me'), and 53:22 calls them by the one word the KJV uses for David himself. Alma 53 is working the David material of 1 Samuel 17-18, and this verse is its Jonathan.

53:2.note: 'He was a man like unto Moroni; and they rejoiced in each other's safety; yea, they were beloved by each other.' No wording is shared, and the row is offered as a type-scene under CONVENTIONS §0a. What lifts it above a guess is recurrence rather than volume: the same twenty verses of 1 Samuel supply the chapter's 'valiant for' at 53:20 and its KJV-singleton 'stripling' at 53:22, so a Jonathan figure at 53:2 is the reading the chapter's own field of allusion predicts.
53:2.whyNot: Nothing verbal at all. If the 1 Samuel 17-18 field claimed for the chapter is declined, this row has no independent support, and 'beloved by each other' is ordinary Book of Mormon diction.

53:17.text: Hereby perceive we the love of God, because he laid down his life for us: and we ought to lay down our lives for the brethren.

provenance.route: 1 John 3:16, with John 15:13 → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: “lay down our lives” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, 1 John 3:16, and “laid down his life” in exactly one, the same verse; “lay down his life” occurs in exactly one, John 15:13. The idiom is confined to the Johannine books. Alma 53:17 nominalizes it — 'unto the laying down of their lives' — and “laying down” occurs in no KJV verse at all, which is what keeps this at moderate rather than high.
provenance.significance: 1 John 3:16 is the KJV's one verse that makes laying down one's life a duty owed by the many to the many: Christ laid down his, 'and we ought to lay down our lives for the brethren.' That is precisely the covenant of Alma 53:17, and the covenanters are the ones for whom it should be hardest. Their fathers swore never to shed blood and were prepared to be slaughtered on that oath (53:11); the sons swear the opposite-looking oath and reach the same place, since 'to protect the land unto the laying down of their lives' is a promise to die rather than to kill. The Johannine verse holds both halves of what the chapter has separated — the fathers' willingness to be killed and the sons' willingness to fight — under one word, and the word is 'brethren', which is what the Lamanites are to the people of Ammon throughout 53:11-13.

53:17.note: 'They entered into a covenant, to fight for the liberty of the Nephites; yea, to protect the land unto the laying down of their lives.' The KJV's only idiom for pledging one's death on another's behalf is the Johannine one, and Alma 53:17 has it in a noun phrase the KJV never forms. Recorded at moderate because the borrowing is of a construction rather than a clause; what makes it worth having is the metalepsis, since 1 John 3:16 supplies exactly the logic that reconciles the sons' covenant with their fathers'. The covenant formula itself ('they entered into a covenant' plus an infinitive of purpose) is 2 Chronicles 15:12's and is adjudicated at Alma 46:35; see the register at this verse.
53:17.whyNot: The shared material is a verbal noun and a possessive, not a clause, and 'laying down of their lives' could be reached from the King James idiom by any nineteenth-century writer steeped in it without a particular verse in mind.

53:21.text: Moreover thou shalt provide out of all the people able men, such as fear God, men of truth, hating covetousness; and place such over them, to be rulers of thousands, and rulers of hundreds, rulers of fifties, and rulers of tens:

provenance.route: Exodus 18:21 (the character list) fused with Acts 26:25 (the phrase) → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: “men of truth” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Exodus 18:21. “truth and soberness” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Acts 26:25, and “soberness” itself in exactly one, the same verse. Alma 53:21's 'they were men of truth and soberness' is the two singletons welded at the shared word.
provenance.significance: Both halves of the weld carry their context in. Exodus 18:21 is Jethro's specification for the men Moses is to set over Israel — able men, God-fearing, men of truth, not covetous — the Bible's one checklist for choosing officers, and Alma 53:20-21 is a checklist for choosing soldiers in exactly that form: valiant, strong and active, true at all times in whatsoever they were entrusted, men of truth and soberness, taught to keep the commandments. Acts 26:25 supplies the other word from the least military scene imaginable: Paul on trial before Agrippa, accused by Festus of being mad, answering that he speaks 'the words of truth and soberness'. Two thousand adolescents going to war are commended in the phrase a prisoner used to prove he was not raving — and 'soberness', a word the KJV uses once in its whole extent, is what the Book of Mormon chooses for teenagers. The book has taken the Bible's standard for magistrates and applied it to children.

53:21.note: 'Yea, they were men of truth and soberness, for they had been taught to keep the commandments of God, and to walk uprightly before him.' Two KJV singletons meet in five words, and neither is decorative: Exodus 18:21 governs the shape of the surrounding list (53:20-21 is a qualifications catalogue, which is what Exodus 18:21 is) and Acts 26:25 governs its wording. The n-gram stream found the Acts half and missed the Exodus half, which is the split-agreement blindness CONVENTIONS §9 describes — 'men of truth' and 'truth and soberness' overlap on one word and no contiguous window sees both.

53:22.text: And the king said, Enquire thou whose son the stripling is.

provenance.other: “stripling” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, 1 Samuel 17:56 — the whole of it being 'And the king said, Enquire thou whose son the stripling is.' The word appears nowhere else in the King James Bible in any form. Separately, “valiant for” occurs in exactly three KJV verses, one of which is 1 Samuel 18:17, Saul's 'only be thou valiant for me, and fight the LORD's battles', said to the same young man twenty verses later; Alma 53:20 reads 'they were exceeding valiant for courage'.
provenance.significance: This is metalepsis of the cleanest kind, because the KJV's single 'stripling' sits inside a question about parentage. Saul, having watched a boy kill a giant, does not ask the boy's name; he asks whose son he is, and 17:58 makes David answer with his father — 'I am the son of thy servant Jesse the Bethlehemite.' Whose sons these two thousand are is the entire content of Alma 53:10-18. They exist in the narrative only as the sons of the people of Ammon; the covenant they can make is defined by the covenant their fathers made and they did not; the book will call them by their fathers for the rest of the war. The one KJV verse containing the word Alma uses for them is the verse in which a king demands to know a young soldier's father — and the answer, in 1 Samuel as in Alma, is the point of the story.

53:22.note: 'Helaman did march at the head of his two thousand stripling soldiers.' A KJV singleton, and one of the most conspicuous single words in the Book of Mormon; 'stripling' is not ordinary nineteenth-century American English for a soldier and the King James Bible uses it once. The chapter has been in this field throughout — Jonathan's love at 53:2, Saul's 'valiant for' at 53:20 — so the borrowing is not an isolated flourish but the naming of a David typology the chapter has already built. Below Skousen's sixteen-word threshold and not one of his 36; the case here rests entirely on the rarity of one word and the aptness of the verse it comes from.
